topic: Topological Sort, Kahn's Algorithm, Disjoint Set Union (DSU), and Minimum Spanning Trees

problems.title: Alien Dictionary
problems.statement:
There is a new alien language that uses the English alphabet. However, the order among letters is unknown to you.

You are given a list of strings `words` from the alien language's dictionary, where the strings in `words` are sorted lexicographically by the rules of this new language.

Return a string of the unique letters in the new alien language sorted in lexicographically increasing order by the new language's rules. If there is no solution, return `""`. If there are multiple solutions, return any of them (deterministic BFS order).

parameterDefinitions.name: words
parameterDefinitions.description: Sorted words list in alien language

constraints: words[i] consists of only lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Pairwise comparisons reveal order: w < e < r < t < f.
Cycle: z < x and x < z, invalid dictionary.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(C) where C is total characters
problems.optimalSpaceComplexity: O(U + min(U^2, N)) where U is unique letters
commonMistakes: Failing to detect prefix invalidity (e.g. ['abc', 'ab']).
Missing letters that appear in words but have no outgoing or incoming edges.
hints: First check if any word is a proper prefix of a previous word: return "" if so.
Compare adjacent words word[i] and word[i+1]. The first differing character gives an edge u -> v.
Perform topological sort using Kahn's algorithm or DFS cycle detection.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=26 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=25 for complexity verification

problems.title: Parallel Courses
problems.statement:
You are given an integer `n`, which indicates that there are `n` courses labeled from `1` to `n`. You are also given an array `relations` where `relations[i] = [prevCourse_i, nextCourse_i]`, representing a prerequisite relationship between course `prevCourse_i` and course `nextCourse_i`: course `prevCourse_i` has to be taken before course `nextCourse_i`.

In one semester, you can take any number of courses as long as you have taken all the prerequisites in the previous semester for the courses you are taking.

Return the minimum number of semesters needed to take all courses. If there is no way to take all the courses, return `-1`.
constraints: All the pairs [prevCourse_i, nextCourse_i] are unique.
commonMistakes: Incrementing semester count per course rather than per BFS layer.
1-based vs 0-based indexing.
hints: In one semester, you can take all available courses whose prerequisites have already been satisfied.
This is standard BFS level-by-level traversal using Kahn's algorithm.
Each level of BFS corresponds to one semester.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Parallel Courses III
problems.statement:
You are given an integer `n`, which indicates that there are `n` courses labeled from `1` to `n`. You are also given a 2D integer array `relations` where `relations[j] = [prevCourse_j, nextCourse_j]` denotes that course `prevCourse_j` must be completed before course `nextCourse_j` can be started (a directed edge).

In addition, you are given a 0-indexed integer array `time` of length `n` where `time[i]` denotes how many months it takes to complete the `(i + 1)-th` course.

You may start taking a course at any time once the prerequisites are met. Any number of courses can be taken at the same time.

Return the minimum number of months needed to complete all the courses.
constraints: The prerequisites graph is a directed acyclic graph (DAG).

examples.explanation: Sem 1: 1 (takes 3) and 2 (takes 2). 3 starts at month 3 and finishes at 3 + 5 = 8.

commonMistakes: Mismatch between 1-indexed course labels and 0-indexed time array `time[u - 1]`.
Summing up times instead of taking max prerequisite completion time.
hints: Dynamic programming on DAG: `maxTime[next] = max(maxTime[next], maxTime[curr] + time[next - 1])`.
Initialize in-degree 0 courses with `maxTime[i] = time[i - 1]`.
The overall minimum time is `Math.max(...maxTime)`.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Minimum Height Trees
problems.statement:
A tree is an undirected graph in which any two vertices are connected by exactly one path. In other words, any connected graph without simple cycles is a tree.

Given a tree of `n` nodes labelled from `0` to `n - 1`, and an array of `n - 1` `edges` where `edges[i] = [ai, bi]` indicates that there is an undirected edge between the two nodes `ai` and `bi` in the tree, you can choose any node of the tree as the root. When you select a node `x` as the root, the result tree has height `h`.

Among all possible rooted trees, those with minimum height are called minimum height trees (MHTs). Return a list of all MHT root labels in ascending order.
constraints: All the pairs (ai, bi) are distinct.
The given input is guaranteed to be a tree and there will be no repeated edges.

examples.explanation: Roots 3 and 4 both yield minimum height 2.

commonMistakes: Calculating tree height from every node independently (O(V^2) TLE).
Not handling n = 1 and n = 2 edge cases.
hints: A tree has at most 2 centroid nodes that minimize maximum path distance.
Trimming leaves: repeatedly prune all nodes with degree 1 until <= 2 nodes remain.
The remaining 1 or 2 nodes are the roots of the minimum height trees.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Sequence Reconstruction
problems.statement:
You are given an integer array `nums` of length `n` where `nums` is a permutation of the integers in the range `[1, n]`. You are also given a 2D integer array `sequences` where each `sequences[i]` is a subsequence of the sequence.

Check if `nums` is the unique shortest supersequence of `sequences`.

Return `true` if `nums` is the unique shortest supersequence of `sequences`, or `false` otherwise.
constraints: nums is a permutation of all the integers in the range [1, n].
All the arrays of sequences are unique.

examples.explanation: [1,3,2] is also a valid supersequence, so [1,2,3] is not unique.

commonMistakes: Failing to check if queue length is > 1 at any moment during topological sort.
Not verifying that the popped elements match nums in exact order.
hints: Construct directed edges for every adjacent pair `seq[i] -> seq[i+1]`.
Perform Kahn's algorithm: at each step, the queue of 0-in-degree nodes MUST have length exactly 1.
If queue has size > 1, multiple valid topological sorts exist -> return false.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification

problems.title: Find Eventual Safe States
problems.statement:
There is a directed graph of `n` nodes with each node labeled from `0` to `n - 1`. The graph is represented by a 0-indexed 2D integer array `graph` where `graph[i]` is an integer array of nodes adjacent to node `i`, meaning there is a directed edge from node `i` to each node in `graph[i]`.

A node is a terminal node if there are no outgoing edges. A node is a safe node if every possible path starting from that node leads to a terminal node (or another safe node).

Return an array containing all the safe nodes of the graph. The answer should be sorted in ascending order.
constraints: graph[i] is sorted in a strictly increasing order.
The number of edges in the graph will be in the range [1, 4 * 10^4].

examples.explanation: Nodes 5 and 6 are terminal nodes. 2 and 4 lead only to 5. 0, 1, 3 are part of or lead to cycles.
Node 4 is the only safe node.
Single node with no edges is terminal (safe).

commonMistakes: Failing to detect self loops `graph[u] = [u]`.
Forgetting to sort the answer in ascending order.
hints: A node is safe if it does not lead to any cycle.
Use 3-color DFS: 0=unvisited, 1=in current cycle, 2=safe.
Alternatively: reverse all edges and run Kahn's algorithm starting from out-degree 0 nodes.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification

problems.title: Redundant Connection II
problems.statement:
In this problem, a rooted tree is a directed graph such that, there is exactly one node (the root) for which all other nodes are descendants of this node, and every node has exactly one parent, except for the root node which has no parents.

The given input is a directed graph that started as a rooted tree with `n` nodes (labeled `1` to `n`), with one additional directed edge added. The added edge has two different vertices chosen from `1` to `n`, and was not an edge that already existed.

Return an edge that can be removed so that the resulting graph is a rooted tree of `n` nodes. If there are multiple answers, return the answer that occurs last in the input.

examples.explanation: Node 3 has two parents (1 and 2). Removing [2,3] restores valid tree.
Cycle exists among 1->2->3->4->1, removing [4,1] breaks cycle.
Node 1 has two parents and a cycle.

commonMistakes: Failing to handle the 3 distinct cases: (1) node with two parents and no cycle, (2) cycle and no node with two parents, (3) node with two parents AND a cycle.
hints: Case 1: Exactly one node has 2 incoming edges (candidate1 and candidate2).
Case 2: A cycle exists with no node having in-degree 2.
Use Union-Find ignoring candidate2. If cycle still occurs, candidate1 is redundant; if no cycle, candidate2 is redundant.

problems.title: Accounts Merge
problems.statement:
Given a list of `accounts` where each element `accounts[i]` is a list of strings, where the first element `accounts[i][0]` is a name, and the rest of the elements are emails representing emails of the account.

Now, we would like to merge these accounts. Two accounts definitely belong to the same person if there is some common email to both accounts. Note that even if two accounts have the same name, they may belong to different people as people could have the same name. A person can have any number of accounts initially, but all of their accounts definitely have the same name.

After merging the accounts, return the accounts in the following format: the first element of each account is the name, and the rest of the elements are emails in sorted order.
constraints: accounts[i][j] (for j > 0) is a valid email.

examples.explanation: The first two John accounts share an email and are merged.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(A * log A) where A is total emails
commonMistakes: Merging accounts solely by name (different people can share the same name).
Forgetting to sort emails alphabetically in each merged account.
hints: Map each email to the account's person name.
Union all emails within the same account with the account's first email.
Group emails by their DSU root, sort each list of emails, and prepend the name.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification

problems.title: Number of Provinces
problems.statement:
There are `n` cities. Some of them are connected, while some are not. If city `a` is connected directly with city `b`, and city `b` is connected directly with city `c`, then city `a` is connected indirectly with city `c`.

A province is a group of directly or indirectly connected cities and no other cities outside of the group.

You are given an `n x n` matrix `isConnected` where `isConnected[i][j] = 1` if the `i-th` city and the `j-th` city are directly connected, and `isConnected[i][j] = 0` otherwise.

Return the total number of provinces.

examples.explanation: Cities 0 and 1 form one province, city 2 forms another.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to initialize provinces count to n.
Checking the entire row including `isConnected[i][i]`.
hints: Initialize provinces = n.
Union city i and city j whenever `isConnected[i][j] === 1`.
Decrement provinces each time a union of two previously separate sets succeeds.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification

problems.title: Regions Cut By Slashes
problems.statement:
An `n x n` grid is composed of `1 x 1` squares where each `1 x 1` square consists of a `'/'`, `'\'`, or blank space `' '`. These characters divide the square into contiguous regions.

Given the grid `grid` represented as a string array, return the number of regions.

Note that backslash characters are escaped, so a `'\'` is represented as `'\\'` in code.
commonMistakes: Subdividing cells into 2x2 instead of 3x3 (2x2 fails because diagonal slashes touch at a single point and cause false leaks).
Forgetting to escape backslashes.
hints: Method 1: Subdivide each cell into 4 triangles (0: top, 1: right, 2: bottom, 3: left). Union based on slash direction and connect across cell boundaries.
Method 2: Upscale each 1x1 cell to a 3x3 pixel grid. Fill slashes with 1s, then run Flood Fill / Number of Islands on 0s.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=25 for complexity verification

problems.title: Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column
problems.statement:
On a 2D plane, we place `n` stones at some integer coordinate points. Each coordinate point may have at most one stone.

A stone can be removed if it shares either the same row or the same column as another stone that has not been removed.

Given an array `stones` of length `n` where `stones[i] = [xi, yi]` represents the location of the `i-th` stone, return the largest possible number of stones that can be removed.
constraints: No two stones are at the same coordinate point.

examples.explanation: One stone can be left in the connected component, 5 removed.

commonMistakes: Failing to separate row coordinate domain from column coordinate domain (e.g. row 0 and col 0 colliding).
Assuming the answer is components instead of stones.length - components.
hints: In each connected component of stones (sharing rows or columns), all stones can be removed except one.
Answer = total stones - number of connected components.
Union row `r` with column `~c` (or `c + 10001`) to distinguish row IDs from col IDs.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification

problems.title: Satisfiability of Equality Equations
problems.statement:
You are given an array of strings `equations` that represent relationships between variables where each string `equations[i]` has length 4 and takes one of two different forms: `"xi==yi"` or `"xi!=yi"`. Here, `xi` and `yi` are lowercase letters that represent single-letter variable names.

Return `true` if it is possible to assign integers to variable names so as to satisfy all the given equations, or `false` otherwise.
constraints: equations[i][0] and equations[i][3] are lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Contradiction: a cannot equal b and not equal b.
a == b and a == c implies b == c, contradicting b != c.

commonMistakes: Processing '!=' before all '==' have been processed.
Not checking self-contradiction `a!=a`.
hints: First pass: process all equality equations `"x==y"` by unioning x and y in a Disjoint Set.
Second pass: process all inequality equations `"x!=y"`. If `find(x) === find(y)`, return false.
If all inequality equations pass, return true.

problems.title: Checking Existence of Edge Length Limited Paths
problems.statement:
An undirected graph of `n` nodes is defined by `edgeList`, where `edgeList[i] = [ui, vi, dis_i]` denotes an edge between nodes `ui` and `vi` with distance `dis_i`. There may be multiple edges between two nodes.

Given an array `queries`, where `queries[j] = [pj, qj, limit_j]`, your task is to determine for each query whether there is a path between `pj` and `qj` such that each edge on the path has a distance strictly less than `limit_j`.

Return a boolean array `answer`, where `answer.length == queries.length` and the `j-th` value of `answer` is `true` if there is a path for `queries[j]` and `false` otherwise.

examples.explanation: For query [0,1,2], limit 2 allows edges < 2 (none, direct edge is 2 so not strictly less). For [0,2,5], path 0-1-2 has edges 2 and 4 < 5 (true).
For [0,4,14], max edge on path is 13 < 14 (true).
Strictly less than limit: 5 < 5 is false.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(E log E + Q log Q)
commonMistakes: Rebuilding the Union-Find from scratch for each query (O(Q * E) TLE).
Using <= instead of < for the distance check (problem specifies strictly less than limit).
hints: Offline queries technique: Sort both edgeList and queries by weight/limit in ascending order.
Iterate through sorted queries; add all edges with weight < query limit to the DSU.
Check `find(p) === find(q)` and store result at the query's original index.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
problems.statement:
You are given an array `points` representing integer coordinates of some points on a 2D-plane, where `points[i] = [xi, yi]`.

The cost of connecting two points `[xi, yi]` and `[xj, yj]` is the manhattan distance between them: `|xi - xj| + |yi - yj|`, where `|val|` denotes the absolute value of `val`.

Return the minimum cost to make all points connected. All points are connected if there is exactly one simple path between any two points.

examples.explanation: MST connects all 3 points with cost 18.

commonMistakes: Using Euclidean distance instead of Manhattan distance |x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2|.
Generating all O(N^2) edges in Kruskal's for large N causing memory overhead when Prim's algorithm in O(N^2) time and O(N) space is optimal for dense complete graphs.
hints: This is a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) problem on a complete graph.
Prim's algorithm with an array runs in O(V^2) time and O(V) space.
Keep track of the minimum distance to connect each unvisited node to the MST.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=35 for complexity verification

problems.title: Number of Operations to Make Network Connected
problems.statement:
There are `n` computers numbered from `0` to `n - 1` connected by ethernet cables `connections` forming a network where `connections[i] = [ai, bi]` represents a connection between computers `ai` and `bi`. Any computer can reach any other computer directly or indirectly through the network.

You are given an initial computer network `connections`. You can extract certain cables between two directly connected computers, and place them between any pair of disconnected computers to make them directly connected.

Return the minimum number of times you need to do this in order to make all the computers connected. If it is not possible, return `-1`.
constraints: No computer is connected to itself.

examples.explanation: Remove redundant wire [1,2] and connect computer 3.
Two extra redundant cables can connect computers 4 and 5.
4 connections is not enough to connect 6 computers (needs >= 5).

commonMistakes: Forgetting that connecting k components requires exactly k - 1 cables.
Not checking `connections.length < n - 1` initially.
hints: To connect n computers, at least n - 1 cables are required.
If `connections.length < n - 1`, return -1 immediately.
Count the number of connected components c using Union-Find. We need `c - 1` operations.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Swim in Rising Water
problems.statement:
You are given an `n x n` integer matrix `grid` where each value `grid[i][j]` represents the elevation at that point `(i, j)`.

The rain starts to fall. At time `t`, the depth of the water everywhere is `t`. You can swim from a square to another 4-directionally adjacent square if and only if the elevation of both squares individually are at most `t`.

You start at the top left square `(0, 0)`. What is the least time until you can reach the bottom right square `(n - 1, n - 1)`?

examples.explanation: At t=3, water level is 3, can traverse (0,0)->(1,0)->(1,1).
Start elevation is 3, cannot swim before t=3.

commonMistakes: Starting binary search from 0 instead of `Math.max(grid[0][0], grid[n-1][n-1])`.
Summing elevations instead of taking the maximum along the path.
hints: Binary search on the answer: range is [max(grid[0][0], grid[n-1][n-1]), n*n - 1].
For a candidate time t, check if (0,0) can reach (n-1,n-1) via BFS using only cells with grid[r][c] <= t.
Alternatively, use Dijkstra's algorithm or Kruskal's with Union-Find.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=15 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification

problems.title: Bricks Falling When Hit
problems.statement:
You are given an `m x n` binary `grid`, where each `1` represents a brick and `0` represents an empty space. A brick is stable if:
- It is directly connected to the top of the grid (`row 0`), or
- At least one of its four adjacent neighboring cells is stable.

You are also given an array `hits`, which is a sequence of erasures we want to apply. Each time we want to erase the brick at the location `hits[i] = (row_i, col_i)`. If there is no brick at that location, no brick drops.

Return an array `result` where each `result[i]` is the number of bricks that fall after the `i-th` erasure is applied.

examples.explanation: Removing brick at (1,0) leaves bricks at (1,1) and (1,2) disconnected from roof, so 2 bricks fall.
First hit removes an edge brick; second hit removes the root of the column, no other bricks drop.
Single brick on roof removed, 0 others fall.

commonMistakes: Applying hits forward (simulating drops forward is O(H * m * n) which TLEs).
Forgetting to subtract 1 for the erased brick itself.
hints: Time-reversal trick: reverse the process by starting from the final grid after all hits are removed, and adding bricks back backwards.
Use Union-Find with a virtual TOP node connected to all row 0 bricks.
When restoring brick at (r, c), the change in TOP component size minus 1 is the number of dropped bricks.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=15 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification

problems.title: Sentence Similarity II
problems.statement:
We can represent a sentence as an array of strings, for example, the sentence `"I am happy with leetcode"` can be represented as `sentence1 = ["I","am","happy","with","leetcode"]`.

Given two sentences `sentence1` and `sentence2` each represented as a string array and given an array of string pairs `similarPairs` where `similarPairs[i] = [xi, yi]` indicates that the two words `xi` and `yi` are similar.

Return `true` if `sentence1` and `sentence2` are similar, or `false` if they are not.

Two sentences are similar if:
- They have the same length (i.e., the same number of words)
- `sentence1[i]` and `sentence2[i]` are similar.

Notice that similarity is transitive: if `a` and `b` are similar, and `b` and `c` are similar, then `a` and `c` are similar.
constraints: sentence1[i] and sentence2[i] consist of lower-case and upper-case English letters.
xi and yi consist of lower-case and upper-case English letters.
commonMistakes: Failing to handle identical words that do not appear in `similarPairs`.
Not checking sentence lengths upfront.
hints: First check if `sentence1.length !== sentence2.length`, return false if not equal.
Build a Disjoint Set Union (DSU) where each similar pair [u, v] is unioned.
For each position i, if sentence1[i] === sentence2[i] or find(sentence1[i]) === find(sentence2[i]), it's valid.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification

problems.title: Lexicographically Smallest Equivalent String
problems.statement:
You are given two strings of the same length `s1` and `s2` and a string `baseStr`.

We say `s1[i]` and `s2[i]` are equivalent characters. Equivalence is an equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, and transitive).

Return the lexicographically smallest equivalent string of `baseStr` by using the equivalency information from `s1` and `s2`.
constraints: s1, s2, and baseStr consist of 'a'-'z'.

examples.explanation: 'p'='m', 'a'='o', 'r'='r', 'k'='r'='m', 'e'='i', 'r'='s'. Smallest equivalent for 'p' is 'm', 'a' is 'a' (or 'a' if 'a' < 'o'), 'r' is 'k' (or 'k' < 'm'/'r'/'s'), giving "makkek".
Equivalences: h=w, e=o, l=r, l=l, o=d. Output is "hdld".
All characters mapped to their smallest equivalent character in each group.

commonMistakes: When unioning two roots `rx` and `ry`, choosing the parent arbitrarily instead of strictly setting `parent[max(rx, ry)] = min(rx, ry)`.
hints: In Union-Find, maintain the invariant that the root of any component is always the lexicographically SMALLEST character in that component.
When unioning rx and ry, if rx < ry, set parent[ry] = rx; otherwise parent[rx] = ry.
For each character c in baseStr, replace with String.fromCharCode(find(c - 97) + 97).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=25 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=26 for complexity verification
